title: A tank drains through a narrowing pipe

stimulus.title: A tank and a narrowing pipe
stimulus.html: A wide, open tank holds water of density ρ. Water flows out through a horizontal pipe at the bottom. The pipe has cross-sectional area A₁ at section 1 and a smaller area A₂ at section 2, where it ends open to the air at atmospheric pressure P₀. The center of the pipe is a depth h below the water surface. The tank is so wide that its surface moves down negligibly slowly. Treat the water as an ideal fluid in a full pipe.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed v₂ of the water leaving section 2. Express your answer in terms of h and physical constants, as appropriate. Begin your derivation by writing a fundamental physics principle or an equation from the reference information.

rubric.point: Starts from Bernoulli's equation (or energy conservation) between the water surface and the exit, with P = P₀ at both and the surface speed negligible
accept: mgh = ½mv² for a parcel of water, with a statement that the pressures at both points are atmospheric

parts.sample: Bernoulli from the surface (point 0) to the exit (point 2), with the pipe's center as y = 0: P₀ + ρgh + ½ρ(0)² = P₀ + ρg(0) + ½ρv₂². Both points are open to the air, so the P₀ terms cancel, and the surface speed is negligible because the tank is wide. ρgh = ½ρv₂², so v₂ = √(2gh).

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the gauge pressure P₁ − P₀ of the water in section 1. Express your answer in terms of ρ, g, h, A₁ and A₂.

rubric.point: Uses continuity to find the speed in section 1: v₁ = (A₂/A₁)v₂
Applies Bernoulli's equation between section 1 and section 2 at the same height

accept: ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) with v₂ = √(2gh) and v₁ = (A₂/A₁)√(2gh) substituted

parts.sample: Continuity (the water is incompressible and the pipe is full): A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so v₁ = (A₂/A₁)√(2gh). Bernoulli between sections 1 and 2, which are at the same height: P₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₀ + ½ρv₂². So P₁ − P₀ = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²) = ½ρ(2gh)[1 − (A₂/A₁)²] = ρgh[1 − (A₂/A₁)²].

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the gauge pressure in section 1 when h = 0.80 m, A₂ = A₁/2 and the fluid is water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³). Use g = 9.8 m/s².

rubric.point: Correct value with units, about 5900 Pa (consistent with the student's part (b) expression)

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The tank is refilled to different depths. On the axes, sketch a graph of the exit speed v₂ as a function of the depth h.

rubric.point: Curve starts at the origin and increases with h
Curve is concave down: it rises ever less steeply, consistent with v₂ ∝ √h (not a straight line)

parts.sample: A curve starting at the origin, rising steeply at first and then less and less steeply (concave down), the shape of v₂ = √(2gh). Four times the depth gives only twice the speed.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: The narrow section is removed, so the pipe has area A₁ all the way to its open end. A student claims that the gauge pressure in section 1 increases, because more water now flows through the pipe each second. Is the student correct? Justify your answer.

rubric.point: States the student is incorrect: the gauge pressure in section 1 decreases (to zero)
Justifies with continuity and Bernoulli: with equal areas, v₁ equals the exit speed, so at the same height P₁ equals the exit pressure P₀; or uses part (b) with A₂ = A₁
accept: no speed change between section 1 and the end, so no pressure difference is needed to accelerate the water

parts.sample: No. With A₂ = A₁, continuity gives v₁ = v₂: the water no longer speeds up between section 1 and the open end. Bernoulli at equal heights then gives P₁ = P₀, so the gauge pressure falls to zero (part (b) with A₂ = A₁ gives ρgh(1 − 1) = 0). The flow rate does increase, but a larger flow does not mean a larger pressure; pressure in section 1 was high only because the water had to be pushed faster into the narrow end.
